title: UX Design Principles for Semi Autonomous Multi Agent Systems — Victor Dibia, Microsoft

primary.label: Agent Architecture & Harnesses

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk is explicitly framed around UX design principles for semi-autonomous multi-agent systems, covering trust, observability, interruptibility, and human-in-the-loop delegation. AutoGen Studio is a developer-facing low-code platform and the design principles are presented as general-purpose guidance for multi-agent systems. Content spans design principles, a five-step build methodology with tools and test beds, and eval-driven iterative improvement. Assumes familiarity with multi-agent concepts and LLM function calling but remains accessible to practicing engineers. Conference presentation featuring live demonstrations of Blender LM and AutoGen Studio. Design principles and quantitative claims are directly grounded in multiple transcript excerpts with specific examples.

summary: Victor Dibia, Principal Research Software Engineer at Microsoft Research with background in human-AI experiences including GitHub Copilot and AutoGen Studio, presents UX design principles for semi-autonomous multi-agent systems (MAS). His earlier LA project (August 2022) demonstrated agentic workflows with error rates dropping from 20% (Da Vinci Codex) to 1.5% (GPT-3.5 turbo). The main demonstration is Blender LM, a multi-agent system built from scratch without frameworks that translates natural language to 3D artifacts in Blender via websocket connections, featuring a planning agent, execution tools, and a verify agent using scene snapshots. Dibia outlines a five-step build methodology: define the goal, create a baseline, build tools (spending ~50% of time on tools), define a test bed (Jupyter notebook, interactive web UI, automated eval suite), and finally build the agent with a base loop, verifier, and planner. He presents four design principles: capability discovery (itemize high-reliability tasks, proactive suggestions), observability and provenance (stream activity logs, debugging tools, token/time metrics), interruptibility (pause, checkpoint, rollback, resume), and cost-aware delegation (estimate action costs, delegate risky actions to users). Dibia cautions that multi-agent systems are not always appropriate and offers a five-step suitability framework: planning benefit, multiple perspectives/personas, extensive context processing, and adaptive solutions requiring reaction to changing environments. He emphasizes eval-driven design—define tasks and metrics first, build non-agent baselines, improve iteratively—and notes academic benchmarks differ from real tasks. He recommends using frameworks rather than building from scratch and references further reading on AutoGen Studio, Magentic One, and Magentic UI.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and Background
sections.summary: Victor Dibia introduces himself as Principal Research Software Engineer at Microsoft Research, with background in human-AI experiences including GitHub Copilot, AutoGen, and AutoGen Studio. Previously worked at Cloud Bear and IBM Research.

sections.title: History: LA Project and Early Agentic Workflows
sections.summary: Describes LA project from August 2022 that enabled data summarization, question generation, code execution, and visualization from CSV/JSON files. Error rate dropped from 20% with Da Vinci Codex to 1.5% with GPT-3.5 turbo, demonstrating early agentic workflow viability.

sections.title: AutoGen and AutoGen Studio
sections.summary: Introduces AutoGen as a multi-agent framework where agents exchange messages and self-organize. AutoGen Studio is a low-code tool for composing multi-agent teams with primitives like models and tools.

sections.title: Blender LM Introduction and Talk Plan
sections.summary: Announces Blender LM as a multi-agent system built from scratch without frameworks for 3D tasks. Outlines talk structure: demo, build walkthrough, design principles synthesis, and takeaways.

sections.title: Background and Motivation for Blender LM
sections.summary: Explains motivation from learning Blender via donut tutorial (4 hours but needs 40-50 hours). Contrasts fixed deterministic workflows with autonomous exploratory systems where LLMs drive control flow. Identifies three characteristics: autonomy, actions with side effects, extended task exploration.

sections.title: Blender LM Live Demo
sections.summary: Demonstrates Blender LM creating two balls with glossy silver finish. Shows websocket connection to Blender, real-time streaming of planning and execution, verify agent taking scene snapshots to assess progress.

sections.title: Build Methodology
sections.summary: Outlines five-step build process: define goal, create baseline, build tools (task-specific and general-purpose, ~50% of time), define test bed (Jupyter notebook, interactive web UI, automated eval suite), then build agent with base loop, verifier, and planner. Emphasizes agents built last.

sections.title: Four Design Principles
sections.summary: Presents four high-level UX design principles: capability discovery (itemize high-reliability tasks, proactive suggestions), observability and provenance (stream logs, debugging tools, token/time metrics), interruptibility (pause, checkpoint, rollback, resume), and cost-aware delegation (estimate action costs, delegate risky actions to users).

sections.title: Key Takeaways: When to Use Multi-Agent and Eval-Driven Design
sections.summary: Cautions multi-agent approaches aren't always appropriate—only a small fraction of tasks truly benefit. Offers five-step suitability framework: planning, multiple perspectives, extensive context processing, adaptive solutions. Emphasizes eval-driven design over building agents first, notes academic benchmarks differ from real tasks, recommends using frameworks, and references further reading on Magentic One, Magentic UI, and his upcoming book.
